pairs.reason: Both claims reference the same tariff program (25%), effective date (May 3), and product scope (safety-critical components). Claim 1 lists specific items (windshields, seat belts) while Claim 2 lists others (seats, batteries); these are overlapping lists rather than contradictory.

Claim 1 states the tariff goes into effect April 2. Claim 2 states it goes into effect for fully assembled vehicles on April 3. This is a direct incompatibility on the effective date for the same product scope.

Both claims describe an exemption for autos/auto parts regarding Mexico/Canada tariffs. Claim 1 specifies an expiry date (April 2), while Claim 2 describes the duration (one-month). These are consistent descriptions of the same policy event.

Claim 1 refers to a 25% tariff effective April/May (implied 2025). Claim 2 refers to a 10% global tariff effective February 24, 2026. These are distinct tariff programs with different dates and scopes.
Both claims are identical in text and metadata regarding the August extension of 50% tariffs on steel/aluminium including car parts. No conflict exists.
Both claims state a 25% tariff on steel/aluminum effective March 12. Claim 2 specifies the year 2025, which aligns with the context of Claim 1.
Both claims identify tariffs on safety parts including seat belts and airbags. Claim 2 provides a broader list of included items (bumpers, mirrors, etc.). They are consistent.
Claim 1 refers to a general 25% tariff on vehicles imported into the US. Claim 2 specifies a reduction to 15% for imports from South Korea announced July 30. These are specific vs general scopes.
Claim 1 states duties will reduce to 15% from a current 25%. Claim 2 states guidance is based on the current 25% rate. These are consistent descriptions of a policy change in progress.

Claim 1 states the tariff applies to non-US content value. Claim 2 states parts remain tariff-free until a process is established to apply tariffs to that same non-US content. These describe the same conditional mechanism.
